A binary search tree is built from
struct Node { int value; std::unique_ptr<Node> left; std::unique_ptr<Node> right; }
, with the usual property: every value under a node's left child is less than the node's own value, and every value under its right child is greater. Write
, which returns the k-th smallest value in the tree, counting from 1, or no value when the tree has fewer than k nodes or k is less than 1. Take
, and visit no more of the tree than it takes to find the answer: O(h + k) time, where h is the tree's height, and O(h) extra space.

This is LeetCode's Kth Smallest Element in a BST. Walking a BST in order visits its values from smallest to largest, so the k-th value that walk produces is the answer, and stopping the moment you have it is what keeps the cost to O(h + k) rather than the O(n) a full traversal pays on a tree far bigger than k. Doing the walk with your own stack, instead of recursion, is what lets the function return as soon as it has an answer: push every node down the left spine, pop one, count it, then push the left spine of its right child.

The edge cases are k below 1, k past the number of nodes, and the empty tree, which the last three lines of output each test.
